title: Fallback penalty matrix — experiment notes (Jun 04 2026)
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a small set of experiments we ran to quantify the user-facing latency penalty and unit-cost delta when the platform executes different fallback strategies. Goal is to create a simple penalty matrix for product/ops to reason about tradeoffs when fast-path capacity is exhausted.

Background / why this matters:
- Customers rely on SLOs (p50/p90/p99) for perceived responsiveness.
- During capacity constraints we can fallback to: (A) smaller/quantized model on same region (model-fallback), (B) route to another region with spare capacity (regional-fallback), (C) queue with short backoff (queue-fallback), (D) degrade feature (e.g., shorten generation length) or (E) execute a cached/approximate response.
- Each option trades latency vs cost vs quality. We need a concise matrix showing expected p99 penalty (ms) and cost delta ($ per 1k queries) for quick operational decisions.

Hypothesis:
1) Model-fallback (quantized) increases p99 modestly (~15–40% depending on sequence length) while reducing cost per token significantly (~20–40%).
2) Regional-fallback increases RTT (network) p99 sharply for geo-sensitive customers but has low CPU/GPU cost delta.
3) Queue-fallback preserves unit-cost but increases tail latency non-linearly under heavy load.

Experiment setup:
- Workload: synthetic chat workload representative of a mid-size app: 60% short-turn (50 tokens), 30% medium (150 tokens), 10% long (500 tokens).
- Traffic shape: steady baseline at 70% capacity with controlled spikes to 140% (6 min windows).
- Models tested: "base-f32" (FP32 baseline), "base-4bit" (quantized, approximation), and "base-compact" (smaller architecture variant).
- Regions: us-central1 (local), europe-west1 (remote).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 generation latency (ms), end-to-end RTT (ms), token cost per request (approx $/1k queries), quality proxy = BLEU-like crude match on canned QA set (higher is better).
- Run length: 3 runs per scenario, aggregate median per metric.

Key numeric results (aggregated medians):

ASCII penalty matrix (p99 increase vs baseline; cost delta per 1k requests)

+----------------------+----------------------+-------------------------+
| Fallback             | p99 increase (ms)    | cost delta ($ / 1k)     |
+----------------------+----------------------+-------------------------+
| model-fallback (4bit)| +120                 | -0.85                   |
| model-fallback (small)| +260                | -1.40                   |
| regional-fallback    | +420                 | +0.05                   |
| queue-fallback (0.5s)| +540                 | 0.00                    |
| degrade-length (trim)| +90                  | -0.30                   |
| cached-approx        | +30                  | -2.10                   |
+----------------------+----------------------+-------------------------+

Notes on the matrix:
- Baseline p99 for base-f32 on same region under these spikes was ~480ms. "p99 increase" above is absolute ms added on top of that baseline.
- Cost delta approximates end-to-end compute + infra cost differences. Negative means cheaper. Cached-approx reduces cost a lot but is only applicable when a cache hit (we enforced 30% hit rate in this sim).
- Regional-fallback additive cost is near zero because we assume similar model runtime billing; network egress and added latency are dominant.

Quality vs savings tradeoff (short summary):
- model-fallback 4bit: quality drop small for short/medium turns (-1.5% quality proxy) but larger for long turns (-6%). Worthwhile when cost pressure is primary.
- model-fallback small-arch: stronger cost savings but more quality loss across the board (~-8% to -12%).
- cached-approx: excellent cost and latency, but only for repeat queries; complexity rises for consistency and freshness.

Mini ASCII charts (session cohort view):
p99 over time (six-minute spike window):
baseline   : ▁▁▂▂▃▄▄▅▅▅▅▅▆▆▆▇▇▇ (peak 480ms)
4bit       : ▁▁▂▃▃▅▅▅▆▆▆▆▇▇▇▇ (peak 600ms)
regional   : ▁▁▂▃▄▅▅▆▆▇▇▇▇▇▇▇ (peak 900ms)
queue-0.5s : ▁▁▁▁▂▂▃▄▅▆▇▇▇▇▇▇ (peak 1020ms)

Interpretation: regional and queue fallbacks create large tail spikes relative to model-fallback or cached responses. If product SLO is p99 <= 1s, queue-fallback can violate this under high contention.

Operational heuristics (first draft):
- If user is geo-sensitive (latency SLO tied to region), prefer model-fallback or degrade-length before regional-fallback.
- If quality is critical (high cost allowed), avoid small-arch model-fallback for long-turn flows.
- Use cached-approx aggressively for idempotent or repetitive queries (search-like or FAQ) — allocate dedicated cache layer and track freshness TTL.
- Queue-fallback should be limited to slow-path non-interactive endpoints or used with explicit client backoff/visibility.

Open questions / risks:
- How representative is the synthetic traffic of customer-specific session mixes? Need to run same scenarios on a small set of real tenant traces (ask CS/SeqEng for two customers).
- Billing model nuance: regional egress costs can change delta sign; need to re-evaluate per-customer pricing profiles.
- Cold-start effects for small-arch variant not fully captured; warmup penalty might increase p99 for the first minute of a surge.
- Cache consistency & privacy risks for cached-approx approach.

Next steps (practical):
1) Run the same matrix with 3 real-customer anonymized traces (action: Daniel K to request traces).
2) Add a sweep across sequence length distributions (focus on >1k token turns) to see small-arch model damage.
3) Prototype a quick runbook in Console that shows "predicted p99 penalty" when operator toggles fallback policy — use numbers from this matrix as initial defaults.
4) Instrument cost attribution per-request (per-route) to better match the cost delta numbers to billing buckets.

Appendix — quick-run config notes:
- Spike generator: open-source loadgen patched to model response size and streaming.
- Cache hit sim: 30% fixed hit rate, TTL 10m.
- Network emulation: added geo-latency + jitter (~60ms baseline to europe-west1, +30–80ms jitter).
- Quality proxy: token-overlap on canned QA (cheap but noisy).

TL;DR: For most interactive workloads we should prefer model-fallback (quantized) or controlled trimming before regional or queue fallbacks. Cached-approx provides best latency/cost if applicable. Use the matrix above as starting defaults for Console policy tool and confirm with a few tenant traces before wide rollout.

Unresolved/notes-to-self:
- Re-run with dynamic warm pools for small-arch model to capture warmup amortization.
- Talk to billing to get precise egress numbers per region for accurate cost deltas.
- Consider adding a combined-policy (trim + 4bit) variant to capture multiplicative effects.
